text: Genesis places seed-bearing vegetation on day three (1:11–13) and the heavenly lights on day four (1:14–19). Reading these as the first physical appearance of plants and the Sun reverses the order in the accepted solar-system formation model.
scope: The strongest disagreement is the Sun–Earth–plants sequence under a literal first-creation reading. A literary arrangement, later visibility of an existing Sun, or miraculous light changes the claim being evaluated; these readings are not established by the scientific sources. Science models natural processes and cannot independently test an unspecified miracle.
summary: On a literal timeline, plants appear before the Sun. Science places the Sun before Earth and its plants.

fields.text: The Sun formed from a collapsing gas-and-dust cloud; planets formed from material in the surrounding disk. Earth’s plants therefore came after the Sun, not before it. This is a conflict about the sequence of natural events, not merely the length of a “day.”

Photosynthesis uses light energy to make sugars from carbon dioxide and water. A naturally developing plant ecosystem needs an energy source. However, Genesis 1:3 already describes light: photosynthesis alone does not prove these plants were in total darkness or that sunlight is the only possible light source.

text: The Sun helps mark days and years; the yearly seasonal cycle relates to Earth’s tilted axis and orbit.
scope: Agreement with observable cycles does not establish the chapter’s creation sequence.
summary: The Sun helps mark days and years. Earth’s tilt and orbit explain the seasonal cycle.

fields.text: Earth’s rotation produces the day–night cycle, and its orbit around the Sun provides the basis of the solar year. These regular motions support the broad observation that heavenly lights can mark time.
The seasonal cycle depends on Earth’s axial tilt as it orbits the Sun. This agreement concerns observable cycles, not the chapter’s order of creation.

text: The day–night pattern broadly agrees with Earth rotating so different regions face toward or away from the Sun.
scope: This is agreement with the observed pattern, not evidence that every detail of the account is scientific.
summary: The day–night pattern agrees with Earth rotating toward and away from the Sun.

fields.text: On a rotating Earth, the side facing the Sun receives daylight and the side turned away experiences night. The verse’s distinction between day and night agrees with this observed pattern; it does not explain the rotation mechanism.

text: If “not be removed” means Earth is physically motionless, that conflicts with Earth’s rotation and orbit around the Sun.
scope: The passage is poetry. Stability or permanence is another reading; the disagreement applies to physical immobility.
summary: If this poem means Earth never moves, it conflicts with Earth’s rotation and orbit. Stability is another possible meaning.

fields.text: Earth spins on its axis and moves around the Sun. A claim that Earth is physically motionless would contradict both motions. The verse is poetry, however: permanence or stability need not mean zero motion.

text: River water reaches the sea and circulates through the water cycle by evaporation, precipitation, and runoff.
scope: Broad observational agreement; the verse does not provide a complete hydrological explanation.
summary: Rivers flowing to the sea broadly fit the water cycle, though the verse does not explain the full process.

fields.text: Water moves through rivers to the ocean and returns to land through evaporation, atmospheric transport and precipitation. This circulation explains why continued river flow does not simply fill the sea without any return process.

text: The image of water rising and returning as rain broadly aligns with evaporation, condensation, and precipitation.
scope: A poetic description, not a complete scientific model.
summary: The poetic description of water rising and returning as rain broadly fits the water cycle.

fields.text: Water evaporates, moves through the atmosphere, condenses and returns as precipitation. The rising-water and rain imagery broadly resembles that circulation. The poem does not specify the complete mechanisms, so this is observational agreement rather than a scientific theory.

text: Josephus describes Herod as a historical ruler of Judea.
scope: Corroborates the ruler and setting; does not independently establish Jesus’s birth or the visit of the magi.
summary: Josephus confirms Herod ruled Judea. This supports the setting, not the birth story itself.

text: Josephus describes Archelaus succeeding Herod and receiving authority over Judea.
scope: Supports the succession. Archelaus’s formal Roman title was ethnarch; it does not independently verify the family’s journey.
summary: Josephus confirms Archelaus succeeded Herod in Judea. This supports the succession, not the family’s journey.

text: Josephus places the census under Quirinius after Archelaus’s removal, which came after Herod’s death. This conflicts with placing that same census in the Herod-era birth setting.
scope: A chronological tension assuming this is the census Josephus describes. Other proposed readings require additional evidence.
summary: Josephus places Quirinius’s census after Herod’s death. Using that census for a Herod-era birth creates a chronological conflict.

text: Josephus records Pilate governing Judea under Tiberius.
scope: Supports those officials and their setting; does not verify every date, title, or named ruler in this verse.
summary: Josephus records Pilate governing Judea under Tiberius. This supports those officials and the setting.

text: Josephus also describes Judas the Galilean’s opposition to the census under Quirinius.
scope: Supports the existence of a census-related movement, not every detail of its leader’s death or followers’ dispersal.
summary: Josephus also describes Judas the Galilean opposing Quirinius’s census. This supports the movement, not every detail of the verse.

title: A solid sky dome?
summary: A literal solid dome holding back an upper sea conflicts with atmospheric science. Whether “firmament” means that dome is an interpretive question.
text: Genesis 1:6–7 describes a divider between waters below and waters above. Paul H. Seely argues that the Hebrew term refers to a solid sky; Vern S. Poythress instead reads the upper waters as rain-bearing clouds. The science comparison below evaluates the solid-dome interpretation, not every possible meaning of the verse.

fields.text: Earth’s atmosphere has gaseous layers that become increasingly thin toward space. A rigid roof enclosing the sky and supporting an upper ocean is incompatible with that measured structure.

Clouds and almost all atmospheric water vapor occur in the lower atmosphere. That differs from a cosmic ocean retained above a solid sky barrier. Water in clouds does not, by itself, conflict with science.

scope: “Snowglobe Earth” is a modern analogy for the dome interpretation, not a phrase or complete model stated in this verse. Verse 6 alone does not establish a flat Earth. The physical dome model disagrees with science; the lexical and literary interpretation remains disputed. This is our conditional assessment, not a NASA judgment on scripture.

title: Celestial lights and the creation sequence
summary: Read as a physical creation sequence, this passage places the Sun after Earth’s vegetation, conflicting with the scientific account. Calling stars “lights” is not itself an error.
text: Genesis 1:11–13 places vegetation on the third day; Genesis 1:14–19 places the making of the celestial lights on the fourth day. Verse 15 describes their role in lighting Earth within that larger account; it does not independently say when stars formed.
scope: This assessment applies to a literal first-creation chronology. A literary or theological reading does not necessarily make the same scientific claim. Reading this as the later visibility of already-existing lights also changes the claim being evaluated; NASA does not establish that interpretation.
reasoning: A literal sequence placing terrestrial vegetation before the Sun conflicts with the solar-system formation model. The issue is the sequence, rather than describing luminous objects as lights.

title: Two animals or seven pairs?
summary: Genesis 6 gives a general instruction to bring pairs; Genesis 7 specifies larger numbers of clean animals and birds.
text: Genesis 6 gives a general instruction to bring pairs; Genesis 7 specifies larger numbers of clean animals and birds.
reasoning: The later distinction can qualify the earlier general rule. Different quantities are present, but the text does not require treating the instructions as mutually exclusive.
scope: This is a comparison of the surviving narrative, not independent confirmation of an ark or flood.

title: Two reasons for the Sabbath
summary: Exodus grounds Sabbath rest in creation; Deuteronomy grounds it in liberation from slavery.
text: Exodus grounds Sabbath rest in creation; Deuteronomy grounds it in liberation from slavery. Deuteronomy 5:14 expressly includes servants’ rest alongside the liberation rationale, giving a social purpose absent from a summary limited to creation.
reasoning: The command to rest is shared, while its stated rationale changes. Both reasons can coexist, so this variation alone is not a logical contradiction.
scope: Textual difference; no claim about which version was historically first.

title: Different legal treatment of servants and slaves
summary: The laws distinguish servants by origin and family status, preserve ownership claims, and specify some release conditions.
text: Leviticus distinguishes impoverished Israelites from foreign slaves inherited as property. It provides redemption and Jubilee release for an Israelite sold to a resident stranger. Exodus also preserves ownership claims over families and specifies injury-related release. Deuteronomy 15 explicitly includes Hebrew women in six-year service release, requires departure provisions and describes remaining permanently through an ear-piercing procedure. These protections remain within its specified servant category. Deuteronomy 23 prohibits returning an escaped servant to the master and allows chosen residence without oppression. Its scope, including whether cross-border escape is implied, is not specified here; the protection should neither be ignored nor treated as an explicit universal abolition law.
reasoning: The broad Jubilee proclamation must be read alongside the explicit foreign-slavery provision. Israelite redemption protections do not establish equivalent release for everyone.
scope: These unequal legal categories do not establish how consistently the laws were practiced. The scope of the broad liberty proclamation merits further study.

title: Where did Aaron die?
summary: Numbers locates Aaron's death on Mount Hor; Deuteronomy names Mosera.
text: Numbers locates Aaron's death on Mount Hor; Deuteronomy names Mosera. Numbers 33 again places Aaron’s death at Mount Hor and lists Moseroth earlier in the itinerary. It does not explicitly identify Moseroth/Mosera with Mount Hor; a regional or retracing explanation needs additional geographical evidence.
reasoning: Read as distinct death locations, these accounts differ. A harmonization could place Mount Hor within a region called Mosera, but the cited passages do not explain that relationship.
scope: A geographical tension in the text; these passages alone cannot settle the historical location.

title: Complete conquest and continuing inhabitants
summary: Broad victory summaries in Joshua sit alongside explicit reports that many inhabitants remained.
text: Broad victory summaries in Joshua sit alongside explicit reports that many inhabitants remained. Exodus 23:29–30 explicitly promises gradual removal rather than completion in one year, adding context to later conquest summaries. Numbers 33 commands dispossession and anticipates failure to remove inhabitants. A command or conditional warning is not itself a report that complete removal occurred. Deuteronomy 7 also pairs commands of complete destruction with gradual removal to prevent wild animals increasing. This reinforces the distinction between a stated goal and the pace or extent of a reported historical occupation. Deuteronomy 20 distinguishes distant-city rules from a destruction command concerning named local nations. This is a prescribed policy and rationale, not a report establishing its completion. Joshua 2:12–21 makes a conditional protection agreement for Rahab’s household: secrecy and remaining in the marked house are specified. Joshua 6:17,22–25 explicitly preserves that household as an exception, linking it to protection of the spies and their oath. Joshua 3:10 presents the coming crossing as assurance of displacement of seven named peoples. It is a promise within the narrative, not a census showing that displacement was completed. Joshua 6:21 describes destruction encompassing people of both sexes and ages and livestock; 6:24 describes burning the city with designated metals preserved for the treasury. The same account orders Rahab and her household brought out alive. These are explicitly differentiated outcomes, so the totalizing statement should be read together with the exceptions rather than quoted in isolation. Joshua 8:24–26 reports destruction of Ai’s inhabitants, while verses 2 and 27 explicitly permit cattle and spoil to be kept. This permission differs from Jericho’s disposal rule and is stated as an exception to treating the cities alike; it is not a claim that all campaigns used one uniform spoil policy. Joshua 10:20 explicitly mentions survivors entering fortified cities after a totalizing battle description. Verses 1 and 6–7 also retain Gibeon as a protected ally. The southern-city destruction reports in 28–40 should therefore be assessed with their stated targets and these exceptions, rather than expanded into an exhaustive population census. Joshua 11 combines a prolonged war (18), a protected Gibeon (19), and Anakim remaining in three named cities (22) with a whole-land summary (23). It also distinguishes killing inhabitants from burning every city: Hazor is singled out for burning, while cattle and spoil are retained (13–14). Neither totalizing victory language nor an absence of a burn layer alone establishes the fate of every settlement. Joshua 12 lists defeated kings associated with Jerusalem, Gezer, Taanach, Megiddo, and Dor. Later inhabitant reports at those places create tension with an exhaustive reading of territorial possession, but defeating a king does not itself assert permanent occupation or extinction of the population. Joshua 13:1 explicitly says much land remains to be possessed, and 13:6 orders allocation while removal of inhabitants is still promised. Verse 13 names peoples not expelled even in the eastern inheritance. Thus assigning land and occupying it are distinguished within Joshua itself. Caleb’s request at 14:12 anticipates his ability to dislodge the Anakim with divine help; 15:14–17 reports local conquests by Caleb and Othniel. These particulars sit beside the earlier Hebron and Anakim victory summaries in 10:37 and 11:21. Their order and scope require interpretation; the future-looking request alone does not prove the same people survived the earlier battle. Joshua 16:10 explicitly retains Gezer’s Canaanites under tribute, while 10:33 describes defeat of Gezer’s king and his assisting force. The earlier military action is not expressly a report that Gezer’s city population was eliminated; applying its no-survivor wording to every later inhabitant would broaden its stated target. Joshua 17:11–13 names towns whose Canaanite inhabitants remain and become tributaries rather than being expelled; the king-list victories therefore do not by themselves establish their permanent depopulation. The Joseph tribes describe iron chariots as an obstacle (16), but Joshua promises successful displacement despite them (18). This is not a statement that God is physically unable to defeat iron chariots. Joshua 18 calls the land subdued while seven tribes still lack their allotments and are urged to take possession (1–3). Survey and lot allocation follow (9–10). The difference between military subjection, administrative allocation and settled possession is explicit; treating these as identical makes the conquest summaries more exhaustive than these particulars support. Jerusalem’s inclusion in Benjamin’s city list (28) is an allotment statement, not a separate report that its remaining Jebusites had been expelled. Joshua 21:43-45 says Israel possessed the entire promised land, received rest, and saw all the good promises fulfilled; 22:4 invokes that rest when releasing the eastern tribes. These statements must be compared with the land still awaiting possession in 13:1-6 and the inhabitants retained in 16:10 and 17:12-13. An exhaustive claim that every promised district was settled and every enemy population removed conflicts with those particulars. A summary of the decisive victory and provision of inheritance has a narrower scope; the distinction is an interpretation of the statements, not proof that every geographical promise was already physically completed. Joshua 23 places remaining nations and future dispossession (4-7) alongside rest, undefeated victory, and fulfilled promises (1,9,14). It warns that future expulsion can cease if Israel abandons the covenant (12-13). Thus even the farewell speech distinguishes present success from future occupation. The congregation in 24:18 again uses a broad removal summary; its scope should not erase the earlier remaining-nation statements. Judges 1:8 reports Judah taking and burning Jerusalem, yet 1:21 reports Benjamin leaving its Jebusites in residence. A raid or capture need not establish permanent expulsion; the passage does not separately narrate a later return. Verse 19 places Judah’s failure against iron-equipped opponents alongside divine assistance: this does not independently establish that God was physically unable to overcome iron. Verses 24-25 explicitly protect the Bethel informant and his family; 27-35 repeatedly describe continued inhabitants and tribute rather than removal. Judges 2:20-23 attributes retained nations to covenant breach and testing, and expressly says they were not delivered into Joshua’s hand. This is a close verbal tension with the universal delivery summary at Joshua 21:44 if both describe every enemy without qualification. A restricted victory-summary reading and the conditional warnings in Joshua 23 give possible distinctions of scope; they do not independently establish how complete the historical occupation was. Judges 3:1-6 retains nations for testing obedience and teaching warfare. These purposes need not exclude the earlier gradual-removal or covenant-judgment explanations; the restrictive wording about teaching war should not be treated as an independently established exclusive cause. Judges 4 again presents a Jabin ruling at Hazor after Joshua 11 names Jabin and reports the king’s death and the city’s burning. The narratives do not identify this as the same individual or say Hazor could never be resettled. Assuming one king creates a chronological conflict; distinct rulers and renewed occupation are possible but their relationship is not narrated. A burn layer alone cannot identify either ruler or date both accounts.
reasoning: Joshua itself preserves an exception at Jerusalem, and Judges lists additional unconquered places. Totalizing military language need not mean every settlement was occupied or every person killed. This explicit exception qualifies an unqualified reading of destruction language; it does not by itself establish the historical extent of conquest or resolve the moral assessment of the killings.
scope: A literal exhaustive reading creates tension; a rhetorical summary of victory allows the stated exceptions. This does not independently date the conquest. Later presence can be explained by incomplete occupation or subsequent return, but these alternatives are not independently demonstrated here. The king list is not a population census or an archaeological chronology. These local accounts may narrate different stages or recap earlier events; their placement alone does not establish a dated sequence.

title: Jabesh Gilead and Saul's public legitimacy
summary: The rescue of Jabesh turns disputed kingship into public recognition; the same town later recovers Saul's body.
text: The rescue of Jabesh turns disputed kingship into public recognition; the same town later recovers Saul's body.
reasoning: Chapter 10 records both acclamation and dissent. Chapter 11 ends with a renewal of kingship after victory. Chapter 31's recovery of Saul's body supplies a later narrative connection to Jabesh.
scope: This is an inference about the narrative's structure, not independent confirmation of the battle, troop totals, or divine intervention.

title: Saul's death: narration and a claimant's story
summary: The narrator says Saul died after falling on his sword; an Amalekite later claims to have killed him.
text: The narrator says Saul died after falling on his sword; an Amalekite later claims to have killed him.
reasoning: The accounts differ, but the second is a character's reported claim. Treating it as a lie for advantage is a possible reading; the story does not require the narrator to endorse every detail of that claim.
scope: An apparent conflict between accounts, with an internal distinction between narration and testimony.

title: Who prompted David's census?
summary: Samuel attributes the prompting to the LORD's anger; Chronicles names Satan.
text: Samuel attributes the prompting to the LORD's anger; Chronicles names Satan.
reasoning: The passages explicitly assign the prompting to different agents. A theological explanation can posit divine permission and an intermediate agent, but neither verse states that combined explanation.
scope: A difference in narrated causation; it does not independently establish a supernatural cause.

title: Seven or three years of famine?
summary: Gad offers David seven years of famine in 2 Samuel and three in 1 Chronicles. The Hebrew has the same two numbers. The Greek of 2 Samuel has three, as Chronicles does.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 24:13: “Shall seven years of famine come unto thee in thy land?” Hebrew (WLC): שֶֽׁבַע שָׁנִ֣ים ׀ רָעָ֣ב [seven years of famine]. KJV 1 Chronicles 21:12: “Either three years' famine”. Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 21:12: שָׁלֹ֨ושׁ שָׁנִ֜ים רָעָ֗ב [three years of famine]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 24:13: εἰ ἔλθῃ σοι τρία ἔτη λιμὸς ἐν τῇ γῇ σου [whether three years of famine shall come to you in your land]. Brenton Greek 1 Chronicles 21:12: ἢ τρία ἔτη λιμοῦ [either three years of famine]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/24/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/21/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA24.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1CH21.htm.
reasoning: Both passages give Gad’s three alternatives after the census, so the numbers are directly comparable. The KJV follows the Hebrew in each book: seven in Samuel, three in Chronicles. Brenton’s Greek has three years in both books, so in Samuel it differs from the KJV.
scope: This extends the published record of the same ID with the Hebrew and Greek wording; the finding between the two KJV verses is unchanged. No claim is made about which number is original. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

summary: Kings lists 40,000 horse stalls; Chronicles lists 4,000, while both list 12,000 horsemen.

summary: Kings gives Ahaziah's accession age as 22; the packaged KJV Chronicles gives 42.
text: Kings gives Ahaziah's accession age as 22; the packaged KJV Chronicles gives 42.

title: Cyrus and restoration of local worship
summary: The Cyrus Cylinder describes restoration of sanctuaries and displaced peoples, providing context for Ezra's account of return.
text: The Cyrus Cylinder describes restoration of sanctuaries and displaced peoples, providing context for Ezra's account of return.

scope: The cylinder is not the Jerusalem decree quoted in Ezra and does not name the Jews or Jerusalem. Compatibility is not direct proof of Ezra's exact decree.

summary: Ezra lists 775 descendants of Arah; Nehemiah lists 652.
text: Ezra lists 775 descendants of Arah; Nehemiah lists 652.

text: Ezra records 2,812 for Pahathmoab's group; Nehemiah records 2,818.

summary: Ezra's itemized figures add to 2,499, while the stated total is 5,400.

title: Approaching or leaving Jericho?
summary: Mark places the blind man's healing on departure from Jericho; Luke places it on approach.
text: Mark names Bartimaeus and locates him as Jesus leaves Jericho. Luke leaves the man unnamed and introduces the encounter as Jesus nears the city.
reasoning: The shared request, crowd rebuke, and healing make these meaningful parallel accounts with a geographical difference.
scope: Separate incidents or distinct city boundaries are proposed harmonizations, but neither explanation appears in these passages.

title: Different qualifications to divorce teaching
summary: The passages share a restrictive view of divorce but state different qualifications.
text: Mark gives an unqualified divorce-and-remarriage prohibition. Matthew includes an exception for sexual misconduct. Paul addresses a departing unbelieving spouse. Deuteronomy 24 describes divorce, a subsequent marriage and a ban on return to the first husband after that marriage ends. Matthew 19:7–8 explicitly discusses Mosaic divorce as a concession rather than the creation ideal. This is an offered interpretation of differing rules, not proof that every divorce statement has identical scope.
reasoning: The texts discuss related but not identical situations; treating one sentence as the entire New Testament rule loses relevant qualifications.
scope: This is a comparison of textual rules, not advice about remaining in an unsafe relationship or a determination of modern legal rights.

title: Resurrection evening and Pentecost
summary: John and Acts present different scenes for receiving the Spirit.
text: John has Jesus breathe on the disciples on resurrection evening. Acts describes waiting for a promised baptism followed by Pentecost.
reasoning: A single-event reading encounters a timing difference; a staged-gift or symbolic-action reading treats the scenes as distinct.
scope: The texts establish the scenes. Choosing a theological relationship between them goes beyond what either explicitly explains.

title: Faith and works in Romans and James
summary: Romans rejects justification by works of the law; James rejects faith without action.
text: Romans emphasizes justification apart from deeds of the law. James describes aid to the needy and Abraham's action as evidence that faith is alive. Rahab provides another linked example: Joshua 2 describes receiving, hiding and redirecting the spies. Hebrews 11:31 associates her survival with faith and receiving them; James 2:25 cites receiving and sending them another way as works.
reasoning: The wording is in tension, but the immediate arguments target different problems: reliance on law and an inactive profession of belief.
scope: Whether these are complementary definitions or divergent emphases is interpretive. The comparison does not establish a scientific claim. These later commendations do not explicitly endorse every statement Rahab made to the pursuers, and reception and action need not be mutually exclusive explanations.

title: A collection with accountability
summary: The letter describes organized material aid and precautions over handling it.
text: Paul presents the collection as a response to need, with companions administering it and concern for public accountability.
reasoning: This is primary textual evidence for the practices the letter advocates; its appeal to manna applies an older narrative to resource sharing.
scope: A letter's description is not an independent audit proving that the collection was completed exactly as planned.

title: Abraham's descendants and Christ
summary: Galatians interprets the promise to Abraham through Christ and then extends it to believers.
text: The chapter first identifies the promised seed with Christ, then calls those belonging to Christ Abraham's seed. Genesis 15 pictures descendants as numerous as stars.
reasoning: This is a theological rereading of a promise about descendants; the chapter itself uses both an individual and a collective application.
scope: The observation concerns interpretation, not a demonstrated factual contradiction.

title: Instructions within a slaveholding household
summary: These instructions address masters and servants within an existing hierarchy.
text: Ephesians commands obedience and limits masters' threats; Colossians requires just treatment; 1 Peter tells servants to endure even harsh masters.
reasoning: The passages regulate relations within the hierarchy rather than explicitly order its abolition. The specific commands differ in emphasis.
scope: This records what these texts prescribe. It neither endorses slavery nor proves how every Christian household behaved.

title: Illness among Christian coworkers
summary: These letters acknowledge serious and continuing illness among coworkers.
text: Philippians says Epaphroditus nearly died and recovered. Second Timothy says Trophimus was left sick at Miletus.
reasoning: The texts do not depict every believer or coworker as immediately cured. They preserve different outcomes without supplying medical diagnoses.
scope: Reported recovery is not clinical evidence identifying its cause, and the passages do not test prayer as a treatment.

title: Shared names and circulating letters
summary: Colossians and Philemon name overlapping people, offering a textual link between the letters.
text: Onesimus, Archippus, Epaphras, Mark, Luke, and Demas occur across the two letters. Colossians also calls for exchanging letters with Laodicea.
reasoning: Shared names support comparison of the social networks represented in the writings; the texts alone cannot establish every biography or resolve authorship debates.
scope: This is internal documentary context, not independent proof that every named person has been identified archaeologically.

title: Expectation and prerequisites for the return
summary: First Thessalonians comforts readers about the dead; Second Thessalonians warns against premature claims about the day.
text: The first passage includes living believers in the anticipated gathering. The second says certain events must precede the day.
reasoning: Their emphases differ, but neither passage supplies a calendar date. The language of expectation should not be converted into a dated prediction without further argument.
scope: This comparison does not settle disputed authorship or whether Paul expected to be alive at the return.

title: Teaching restrictions and women's prophecy
summary: First Timothy restricts women's teaching; other passages envision women praying or prophesying.
text: First Corinthians discusses the manner in which women prophesy, while Acts applies a promise of prophecy to daughters and female servants.
reasoning: A blanket claim that all female religious speech is forbidden does not capture all these passages. Distinguishing prophecy from authoritative teaching is one interpretive response.
scope: The texts support a difference in permissions and activities; they do not by themselves settle modern debates over ordination.

title: Grace and practical assistance
summary: Titus distinguishes salvation from righteous works while also requiring useful good works.
text: Within one chapter, salvation is attributed to mercy and believers are urged to meet practical needs through good work. James likewise criticizes words of care without assistance.
reasoning: The local context prevents treating the rejection of salvation by works as a rejection of ethical action.
scope: This is an internal comparison of ethical and theological language, not evidence that either theological claim is empirically proven.

title: Onesimus: brotherhood and freedom
summary: Philemon asks for Onesimus to be received as a brother but does not explicitly record a completed emancipation.
text: The appeal addresses return, consent, possible debt, and a relationship beyond servitude. Its expectation that the recipient will do more remains unspecified.
reasoning: A request for brotherly reception is present; a formal legal release and its outcome are not narrated.
scope: Readers may infer an appeal toward freedom, but the letter alone does not establish that Onesimus was emancipated.

title: Jeremiah's promise interpreted in Hebrews
summary: Hebrews uses Jeremiah's new-covenant promise to argue that the first covenant is becoming obsolete.
text: Jeremiah addresses Israel and Judah and describes internalized law. Hebrews quotes that promise in an argument about Jesus's priestly ministry.
reasoning: The later text makes a Christian interpretive move from the word new to the status of the earlier covenant.
scope: This identifies the argument within Hebrews; it does not present its Christian conclusion as a neutral description accepted by all Jewish readers.

title: Explaining the delayed return
summary: Second Peter explicitly addresses objections that the promised return has not occurred.
text: The reply appeals to divine time and patience and urges ethical readiness. The comparison of a day and a thousand years appears in that argument.
reasoning: Reading the comparison as a fixed mathematical conversion for dating creation or the end ignores its function as an answer to delay.
scope: This is a textual interpretation of the argument, not a measurement of cosmological time or scientific confirmation of future destruction.

title: Confession and claims about sinlessness
summary: First John warns against denying sin, yet also says those born of God do not sin.
text: The first chapter calls for confession; the third contrasts God's children with patterns of wrongdoing.
reasoning: An absolute sinlessness reading creates tension. A reading about settled conduct versus individual failures is one way to interpret the passages together.
scope: The distinction is an interpretation of the context, not wording explicitly supplied by these English verses.

title: Hospitality and disputed teachers
summary: Second John restricts hospitality to certain teachers; Third John condemns refusal to welcome approved workers.
text: The two letters use hospitality to mark different boundaries of community membership and authority.
reasoning: Their commands are not unconditional opposites: they evaluate different visitors. The important question is who the author regards as a legitimate representative.
scope: This concerns the letters' internal criteria, not an independent judgment that their opponents were deceptive.

title: Clouds, trees, waves, and wandering stars
summary: Jude uses natural images to criticize people, rather than give a scientific account of weather or astronomy.
text: Its sequence of comparisons includes fruitless trees, foaming waves, and wandering stars, all applied to the disputed people discussed in the letter.
reasoning: The referents are human opponents and their conduct; treating every image as a physical proposition mistakes the passage's rhetorical function.
scope: This does not evaluate the historical identity of the opponents or verify the letter's moral allegations.

title: Stars and lamps explicitly interpreted as symbols
summary: Revelation itself explains its seven stars and seven lampstands symbolically.
text: Verse 20 identifies the stars with angels of churches and the lampstands with the churches.
reasoning: The explicit explanation supplies a strong contextual reason not to read these particular stars as a claim about stellar size or physical placement.
scope: This conclusion applies to this vision; it is not a blanket scientific or historical verdict on every image elsewhere in Revelation.

title: Cosmic poetry uses several images
summary: Job describes earth suspended over nothing alongside heavenly pillars and a defeated cosmic serpent.
text: The speech places suspended earth, clouds holding water, heavenly pillars, and a fleeing serpent side by side.
reasoning: Calling verse 7 a modern astronomical prediction while treating adjacent images figuratively applies inconsistent standards.
scope: Poetic portrayal of divine power, not a complete physical model.

title: The book corrects its own speakers
summary: The ending rejects what Job’s friends said about God.
text: God rebukes Eliphaz and his two companions and directs them to seek Job’s intercession.
reasoning: A character’s statement should not automatically be treated as the final position of the book. Speaker and narrative outcome matter.
scope: Internal literary assessment; does not verify historical conversations.

title: Exile, grief, and violent retaliation
summary: This lament moves from captivity in Babylon to a wish for retaliation against Babylonian children.
text: The poem remembers Zion, accuses Edom of encouraging destruction, and ends by blessing violent retaliation.
reasoning: The final violence is the speakers’ wish within a lament. Genre identifies the speaker without removing the ethical difficulty.
scope: Literary memory does not independently corroborate or date every event.

title: Opposite advice in adjacent sayings
summary: One proverb says not to answer a fool; the next says to answer one.
text: Verse 4 warns that answering can make the respondent like the fool; verse 5 warns that silence leaves the fool self-satisfied.
reasoning: As unconditional rules they conflict; their differing reasons also permit advice for different circumstances.
scope: A verbal tension; judgment depends on whether proverbs are treated as universal commands.

title: Death in wisdom and apocalyptic texts
summary: Ecclesiastes describes inactive dead; Daniel anticipates their awakening.
text: Ecclesiastes says the dead no longer participate in what happens under the sun and describes Sheol as without work or knowledge. Daniel 12:2 describes resurrection.
reasoning: The texts conflict if Ecclesiastes denies all future existence, but its repeated earthly perspective permits a distinction between present inactivity and future awakening.
scope: Literary comparison, not empirical verification of an afterlife.

title: Figurative language in love poetry
summary: Goats, sheep, fruit, towers, and deer praise a lover through comparisons.
text: Hair is compared to goats, teeth to sheep, temples to pomegranate, and the neck to a tower.
reasoning: The repeated comparative language marks a poetic portrait rather than biological claims. Later allegorical readings add interpretive frameworks.
scope: Genre context; does not settle authorship or later religious interpretation.

title: Assyrian campaign and Hezekiah
summary: An Assyrian inscription independently names tribute from Hezekiah in 701 BCE.
text: Isaiah places Sennacherib’s forces in Judah and at Lachish. The British Museum catalog records a Sennacherib prism describing tribute from Hezekiah in 701 BCE.
reasoning: Independent royal evidence supports the rulers and political setting; speeches and miraculous deliverance still require separate evaluation.
scope: Corroboration of setting, not the complete narrative.

title: Cyrus and independent royal evidence
summary: Cyrus is independently attested; his divine commissioning is Isaiah’s theological claim.
text: Isaiah calls Cyrus an anointed ruler. The Cyrus Cylinder records conquest of Babylon and restoration of shrines and displaced peoples.
reasoning: The artifact supports the ruler and broader policy. It does not name the Jews, date Isaiah’s composition, or verify divine commissioning.
scope: Historical evidence and claims about prophecy must be distinguished.

title: Conditional prophetic warnings
summary: Jeremiah explicitly allows announced destruction or blessing to change with conduct.
text: The potter illustration leads to two conditions: repentance can avert threatened judgment; disobedience can cancel promised good.
reasoning: Evaluation of a prediction should consider whether its own framework makes it conditional. This cannot be assumed for every oracle.
scope: Textual explanation, not a blanket exemption from historical evaluation.

title: Inherited suffering and individual guilt
summary: Lamentations describes bearing ancestors’ wrongdoing; Ezekiel rejects inherited guilt.
text: Lamentations 5:7 describes descendants suffering from ancestors’ actions, while verse 16 also acknowledges their own sin. Ezekiel assigns guilt to the acting person.
reasoning: The wording is in tension but can distinguish inherited consequences from individual responsibility.
scope: A lament need not be a systematic doctrine of punishment.

title: Responsibility and change
summary: Ezekiel assigns responsibility individually and allows changed conduct to change the outcome.
text: Children do not bear parents’ guilt. Subsequent verses say a wicked person may turn, while a righteous person may abandon righteousness.
reasoning: The opening sour-grapes proverb explains why intergenerational responsibility is central to the argument.
scope: Internal interpretation; compare collective consequences without equating them with guilt.

title: Tyre campaign: an internal qualification
summary: A later oracle says Nebuchadnezzar received no reward from his Tyre campaign.
text: Ezekiel 26 names Nebuchadnezzar and anticipates destruction and plunder. Ezekiel 29 says his army received no wages there and presents Egypt as compensation.
reasoning: The texts complicate an uncomplicated fulfillment claim. Chapter 26 changes from singular to plural agents, requiring care about who is said to fulfill each line.
scope: Internal tension; these verses alone do not reconstruct the entire siege.

title: Resurrection in an end-time vision
summary: Daniel connects awakening from death with crisis and final justice.
text: Distress is followed by rescue, resurrection to different destinies, and the wise shining like stars.
reasoning: The star wording is a comparison within a vision, not a physical description of transformed human bodies.
scope: Apocalyptic claim; this is not an empirical demonstration of resurrection.

title: Mercy and ritual
summary: Hosea prioritizes enduring loyalty and knowledge of God over offerings.
text: The comparison with fleeting dew precedes the declaration favoring mercy over sacrifice.
reasoning: The immediate criticism concerns unreliable loyalty and ritual as a substitute for faithfulness; it need not prohibit every sacrifice.
scope: Prophetic ethical rhetoric in its context.

title: Locust and army imagery
summary: Joel describes devastation with military comparisons and later calls locusts God’s army.
text: The invaders look like horses, move like warriors, and enter houses; verse 25 explicitly refers to locusts.
reasoning: The repeated comparisons support agricultural and poetic readings. The passage does not identify a modern army or a dated astronomical event.
scope: Interpretations vary over literal plague and symbolic invasion.

title: Worship rejected without justice
summary: Amos juxtaposes rejected rituals with a demand for justice.
text: Feasts, offerings, and songs are rejected before the demand for justice and righteousness to flow like water.
reasoning: The contrast is ethical; its river language is metaphorical, not hydrological. Hosea and Micah offer related critiques.
scope: Primary-text comparison, not independent verification of divine speech.

title: Edom at Jerusalem’s catastrophe
summary: Obadiah accuses Edom of assisting or exploiting Judah’s disaster.
text: The accusation includes rejoicing, looting, intercepting escapees, and handing over survivors. Psalm 137 also associates Edom with Jerusalem’s destruction.
reasoning: The shared theme connects two literary memories but does not establish their independence or composition dates.
scope: Exact event identification and external corroboration require more evidence.

title: A threatened destruction is averted
summary: Jonah’s forty-day warning is followed by repentance and an explicitly averted disaster.
text: The king calls for an end to violence, and the narrator says God sees the changed conduct and does not carry out the destruction.
reasoning: The reversal is the story’s stated outcome. Jeremiah offers a related principle of conditional warnings.
scope: Literary claim; not independent evidence for a historical citywide conversion.

title: The narrative challenges Jonah
summary: Jonah resents mercy for Nineveh; the closing question defends concern for its people and animals.
text: Jonah says he fled because he knew God was merciful. The plant episode contrasts his concern for shade with his hostility toward the city.
reasoning: The prophet’s attitude is not the narrator’s unquestioned position. The ending must be included when interpreting the warning.
scope: Literary reading; the stated population is not independently established.

title: A peace oracle shared with Isaiah
summary: Micah and Isaiah have closely parallel wording about weapons becoming farming tools.
text: Both describe nations coming to Zion, instruction from Jerusalem, judgment between peoples, and an end to learning war.
reasoning: The verbal overlap is direct evidence of a textual relationship, but does not alone identify a borrower or exclude a common tradition.
scope: Textual comparison; future peace is not a description of present conditions.

title: Extreme offerings and the ethical response
summary: Questions about escalating offerings end with a call to justice, mercy, and humility.
text: The questions move from calves to thousands of rams, rivers of oil, and a firstborn child. Verse 8 gives the response.
reasoning: The firstborn question is not an instruction to sacrifice children; it belongs to an escalating rhetorical contrast.
scope: Does not establish how prevalent any ancient ritual was.

title: Nineveh compared with No-Amon
summary: Nahum warns Nineveh by recalling another city’s defeat.
text: The passage describes No-Amon’s defenses and allies, followed by captivity and violence against its inhabitants.
reasoning: The analogy argues that power and alliances cannot guarantee protection. The hostile oracle is not an impartial campaign report.
scope: Primary textual setting; this note does not independently date the conquest.

title: Cosmic imagery in a warrior poem
summary: Sun, moon, rivers, and mountains participate in a poetic picture of divine warfare.
text: The prayer describes divine chariots, arrows, and trampling the sea; mountains see and fear, and the deep raises its hands.
reasoning: Personification and martial imagery make genre essential before judging individual lines as physical claims.
scope: Poetic context, not empirical confirmation of a stopped Sun or Moon.

title: Sweeping judgment and a surviving remnant
summary: Universal destruction language is followed immediately by peoples worshiping and survivors.
text: Verse 8 describes all earth consumed; verses 9-13 describe purified peoples, offerings, and an afflicted remnant.
reasoning: The continuation complicates an interpretation in which every person is physically destroyed. Comprehensive rhetoric coexists with restoration.
scope: Internal context; does not identify a particular future physical event.

title: Temple rebuilding and drought
summary: Haggai attributes poor harvests to neglect of the temple in a dated prophetic appeal.
text: The passage names Darius’s second year, Zerubbabel, and Joshua, then interprets drought and poor returns as consequences of neglect.
reasoning: Named officials and a regnal date frame the narrative; divine causation of weather is the oracle’s explanation rather than independently demonstrated meteorology.
scope: Distinguishes a historical frame from a verified causal mechanism.

title: Fasting, collective memory, and justice
summary: A question about mourning becomes a critique of oppression and refusal to listen.
text: The answer questions whom the fasting served, then recalls obligations toward widows, orphans, foreigners, and the poor.
reasoning: The passage connects ritual memory with moral responsibility, providing a theological interpretation of devastation.
scope: Primary textual context, not independent proof of the cause of exile.

title: Tithes in an agricultural setting
summary: The promised blessing concerns food stores, crops, vines, and crop destroyers.
text: The community is accused of withholding tithes; the response promises provision and protection for produce.
reasoning: Its agricultural setting matters. A guaranteed modern investment return is an extension beyond the immediate text.
scope: Theological promise, not a financial or scientific guarantee.

title: Seventy or seventy-five family members?
summary: Exodus and Genesis give a family total of seventy; Stephen’s speech in Acts gives seventy-five. The Septuagint also reads seventy-five in Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5.
text: Exodus 1:5 gives seventy descendants and notes Joseph was already in Egypt. Genesis 46:26–27 distinguishes sixty-six traveling descendants from a total household of seventy. Acts 7:14 gives seventy-five for the relatives Joseph summoned. Original-language wording: the Hebrew (WLC) has שִׁבְעִֽים [seventy] at Genesis 46:27 and שִׁבְעִ֣ים נָ֑פֶשׁ [seventy souls] at Exodus 1:5, which the KJV follows (“threescore and ten”; “seventy souls”). The Brenton Greek of Genesis 46:27 gives Joseph nine sons, not two, and a total of seventy-five: ψυχαὶ ἐννέα … ψυχαὶ ἑβδομηκονταπέντε; its Exodus 1:5 has πέντε καὶ ἑβδομήκοντα [seventy-five]. Acts 7:14 (KJV “threescore and fifteen souls”) reads ἐν ψυχαῖς ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε in the SBL and Tischendorf editions, and the same words in the Textus Receptus. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/46/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN46.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO01.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/SBLGNT/44/7/.
reasoning: The totals differ in all three packaged translations. The passages do not describe their counting categories in identical terms, so the numerical difference is directly visible while its explanation needs further evidence.
scope: This records an apparent textual discrepancy. Counting scope and textual transmission are questions for further research; these citations alone do not establish a particular reconciliation or manuscript history. Stephen’s seventy-five agrees with the Septuagint of Genesis and Exodus and disagrees with the Hebrew those KJV chapters translate. This shows where the two figures sit in the named editions; it does not show which figure is earlier or how either was counted. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier.

title: Royal orders and the rescue of children
summary: The midwives refuse Pharaoh’s order to kill boys; Pharaoh’s daughter later rescues a Hebrew child.
text: Exodus 1:16–22 moves from an order to the midwives to a general command to drown male infants. The midwives preserve the children and are commended for fearing God. In Exodus 2:5–10, Pharaoh’s daughter recognizes a Hebrew baby, arranges nursing and adopts him.
reasoning: The two chapters contrast royal policy with the choices of named midwives and a member of the royal household. Reading them together shows that the narrative does not portray every Egyptian as carrying out the king’s order.
scope: This is an internal narrative comparison, not independent confirmation of an Egyptian decree, the identity of a pharaoh or the historicity of the rescue. The midwives’ explanation in 1:19 is a character’s statement, not medical evidence about childbirth.

title: When was the divine name known?
summary: Exodus 6 says the patriarchs did not know God by the name Jehovah; Genesis presents that name in speech to Abram.
text: Exodus 3:13–15 connects the name revealed to Moses with the God of the patriarchs. Exodus 6:2–3 contrasts appearing as God Almighty with being known by the name Jehovah. In Genesis 15:7, the speaker identifies himself to Abram using the name rendered Jehovah in ASV and LORD in WEB.
reasoning: If being known means knowing the name itself, the statements are in tension. An experiential reading—coming to know the name’s significance through deliverance—changes the comparison. The English editions also render the name differently, making the ASV wording useful to compare.
scope: This is an interpretive tension. The cited passages do not prove an experiential reconciliation or a particular theory about how the texts were composed. The packaged KJV normalizes some LORD capitalization; typography alone should not decide the issue.

title: Signs offered to establish a messenger’s authority
summary: The staff, changed hand and water-to-blood signs answer Moses’s fear that people will not believe him.
text: Exodus 4:1–9 presents extraordinary transformations as signs of divine commissioning. Verses 5 and 8–9 explicitly describe their purpose as eliciting belief. In 4:30–31, Aaron performs signs before the people and they believe.
reasoning: The narrative itself identifies an evidentiary purpose for the signs. It does not give a repeatable procedure, physical explanation or independent observation that could be tested from this account.
scope: Calling an event a miraculous sign does not establish its occurrence or a natural mechanism. These verses alone also do not justify a modern medical diagnosis from the translated description of the hand. This is context for the claim, not scientific confirmation or a claim that science disproves every miracle.

title: An abrupt threat during the return journey
summary: After commissioning Moses, the narrative describes a lethal divine encounter ended by Zipporah’s circumcision of her son.
text: Exodus 4:19–23 sends Moses back to Egypt and announces a confrontation with Pharaoh. The following scene, 4:24–26, says the LORD sought to kill him, then describes Zipporah circumcising her son and the threat ending.
reasoning: The scene creates a striking interruption in the commission. The short account does not explicitly explain the offense or clearly name the referent of every pronoun. Circumcision is the action narrated immediately before release.
scope: A link to neglected circumcision is an interpretation of the sequence, not a fully stated explanation in these verses. Do not present a guessed identity for every pronoun or a reconstructed motive as settled fact.

title: Belief gives way to distress under heavier labor
summary: The people first believe the promise of rescue, but harsher labor leads to blame and refusal to listen.
text: Exodus 4:31 records belief. After Pharaoh removes straw supplies while keeping brick quotas in Exodus 5, the officers blame Moses and Aaron, and Moses questions the failed rescue. Exodus 6:9 explicitly attributes the people’s refusal to listen to anguish and harsh bondage.
reasoning: The changing response has a stated narrative cause. Exodus 3:19–20 had already anticipated Pharaoh’s resistance, so the worsening conditions are a setback within the narrative rather than a simple contradiction of a promise of immediate success.
scope: The chapters describe coercive labor and suffering but do not independently identify the ruler, date the events or establish the scale of the workforce. A literary explanation of changed belief is not historical corroboration.

title: Who hardens Pharaoh’s heart?
summary: The narrative attributes Pharaoh’s resistance both to Pharaoh himself and to God.
text: Exodus 7:3 announces divine hardening. Exodus 8:15 and 8:32 explicitly say Pharaoh hardens his own heart; 9:12 attributes hardening to the LORD, while 9:34 again names Pharaoh and his servants. Exodus 10:1–3 places divine hardening beside a demand that Pharaoh humble himself. Exodus 14 again juxtaposes divine hardening (14:4,8,17) with Pharaoh and his servants regretting the release of their workforce (14:5).
reasoning: These are different assignments of agency within the same narrative. They are not automatically mutually exclusive, but they raise a question about how responsibility and divine intervention are related.
scope: The verses do not supply a complete theory of free will. A claim that God only hardens an already resistant ruler must also account for the advance announcement; a claim that Pharaoh has no agency must account for passages assigning action and blame to him.

title: Imitation gives way to inability
summary: Egyptian magicians imitate early signs but later fail and become afflicted themselves.
text: Exodus 7:11–12 and 7:22 attribute similar signs to Pharaoh’s magicians, and 8:7 says they bring up frogs. In 8:18–19 they fail to reproduce the next sign and acknowledge divine power. In 9:11 boils prevent them from standing before Moses.
reasoning: The account changes the magicians’ role from rival performers to witnesses of their limits. It does not treat every supernatural-looking action as unique to Moses and Aaron.
scope: This identifies a literary progression. The text does not explain the magicians’ methods, prove a modern stage-illusion reconstruction, or independently verify supernatural powers.

title: Livestock after “all” have died
summary: After saying all Egyptian livestock died, Exodus describes livestock threatened by later plagues.
text: Exodus 9:6 describes all Egyptian livestock dying. Yet 9:19–21 tells Egyptians to shelter livestock before the hail, and 11:5 and 12:29 refer to firstborn animals. The earlier warning in 9:3 specifically names livestock in the field.
reasoning: An unrestricted reading of all creates a continuity problem. Reading it within the field-livestock scope of 9:3 offers a possible explanation, because the hail warning explicitly distinguishes sheltered and exposed animals.
scope: The narrative does not explicitly list survivors of the earlier plague or say that replacement animals were purchased. The field qualification is present in the text; a replenishment story would require additional evidence.

title: What remained for the locusts?
summary: The broad description of hail damage is qualified by a later statement that some crops survived.
text: Exodus 9:25 describes hail striking every field plant and breaking every tree. Verses 31–32 distinguish damaged flax and barley from wheat and the other later crop, which were not struck. Exodus 10:5, 10:12 and 10:15 explicitly describe locusts eating what the hail left.
reasoning: The nearby crop-specific qualification matters when assessing the sweeping wording. Reading the summary as absolute destruction of all vegetation ignores an exception stated within the same chapter.
scope: This resolves one apparent narrative tension through explicit context. It does not independently confirm the agricultural season, identify every ancient crop term, or verify the plague as a historical event.

title: Wind and locust migration
summary: Wind-driven locust movement fits observed swarm behavior; it does not verify this particular plague.
text: Exodus 10:13 attributes the arrival of locusts to an east wind; 10:19 describes their removal by a strong west wind. FAO explains that desert locusts generally travel with the wind and can migrate long distances.
reasoning: Wind-assisted migration is an independently documented biological behavior. This supports that limited feature of the description, rather than the entire sequence of events.
scope: FAO’s observations do not identify the species in this ancient account, date the event, verify its unprecedented scale or confirm divine timing and the complete removal of every locust.

sources.label: FAO · Desert Locust movement and behavior

title: Would Moses see Pharaoh again?
summary: Moses says he will not see Pharaoh again, yet the narrative continues with a warning and a later summons.
text: Exodus 10:28–29 ends with Pharaoh banning another audience and Moses agreeing. Exodus 11:4–8 gives the firstborn warning and ends with Moses leaving Pharaoh. Exodus 12:31 reports that Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron during the night.
reasoning: The warning in chapter 11 can be read as a continuation of the same audience, because departure is narrated only at 11:8. The later summons raises a further question, but 12:31 does not describe the mechanics of delivering the message.
scope: Chapter divisions alone do not establish a new encounter. Neither a direct final meeting nor an exclusively messenger-delivered summons is fully described here. Do not present one reconstruction as established by these verses.

title: An escape story becomes a recurring observance
summary: Passover instructions connect household ritual, the departure narrative and explanation to future children.
text: Exodus 12:14 and 12:24–27 prescribe continuing observance and an answer to children who ask its meaning. The same chapter describes departure in haste and dough that had not risen in 12:34 and 12:39. Exodus 13:8–10 and 13:14–16 continue the connection between observance, memory and teaching children. Deuteronomy 16 again connects unleavened bread with the remembered departure and forbids overnight leftovers; its six days plus seventh-day assembly retain a seven-day framework.
reasoning: The chapter presents a ritual with an explanation rooted in the narrated rescue. It combines instructions for commemoration with the story those instructions ask later generations to remember.
scope: A text prescribing a recurring festival does not independently establish when every element of the festival originated, how uniformly it was practiced or the historicity of the departure.

title: Excluding foreigners and admitting a sojourner
summary: Passover rules exclude some outsiders but explicitly allow a circumcised sojourner to participate.
text: Exodus 12:43 prohibits participation by a stranger, and 12:45 excludes a foreigner and hired servant. Verse 48 then gives a condition under which a sojourner may participate and be treated as native-born. Verse 49 states one law for the native and sojourner.
reasoning: The immediate context distinguishes an outsider who does not meet the participation condition from one who does. Treating every English outsider term as an unconditional, identical category creates an avoidable contradiction.
scope: The condition is explicitly stated in this ritual law. This does not establish equal social status in every other law or erase the separate rules about purchased servants in verse 44.

title: Firstborn people are redeemed, not offered as animals
summary: The firstborn dedication includes explicit redemption of human children and a separate rule for donkeys.
text: Exodus 13:2 dedicates firstborn humans and animals. Verses 12–15 distinguish animal offerings, a donkey redeemed with a lamb or killed, and human firstborn who must be redeemed. Exodus 22:29–30 gives a general firstborn dedication command. Exodus 13:13–15 explicitly supplies human redemption, so dedication should not automatically be equated with human sacrifice. Exodus 34:19–20 repeats the distinction between firstborn dedication and redeeming sons. Numbers 3 describes Levites substituting for Israelite firstborn and a payment for the excess firstborn. Numbers 18 again mandates redemption of firstborn people and unclean animals, contrasting cattle, sheep and goats that are not redeemed.
reasoning: The general dedication must be read with the specific human-redemption rule. Verse 15 explicitly contrasts animal sacrifice with redeeming the speaker’s children. This is an additional substitution and redemption procedure, not an instruction to kill those firstborn.
scope: These verses establish the rule this passage gives. They do not independently reconstruct every ancient practice or settle how redemption was administered in each period.

title: A modeled wind effect is not proof of a crossing
summary: Strong wind can expose shallow terrain in a model; the proposed location and conditions remain assumptions.
text: Exodus 14:21 describes an east wind acting overnight, and 14:22–29 describes passage between waters and their return. Drews and Han (2010) modeled wind setdown in reconstructed eastern Nile-delta terrain. Their 28 m/s east-wind experiment exposed a temporary land bridge for about four hours.
reasoning: The study demonstrates a hydrodynamic possibility under specified geography and forcing. It is a model experiment, not an observation of Moses’s crossing.
scope: The model does not establish the biblical site, ancient weather, participants or event. Its shallow-basin results should not be generalized to arbitrary deep-water locations or treated as verification of every narrative detail.

sources.label: Drews & Han (2010) · Wind setdown model, PLOS ONE

title: A victory song uses bodily and landscape imagery
summary: The song retells the sea rescue with images of a divine hand, nostrils and the earth swallowing enemies.
text: Exodus 15 identifies the passage as a song. Its account of the victory includes a warrior description, a right hand, a blast from nostrils and the earth swallowing enemies. Verse 19 returns to a prose summary of waters covering the Egyptian forces.
reasoning: Genre matters: the song’s figurative language and its prose summary describe the victory in different forms. Treating every body-part image as a literal anatomical claim overlooks the explicitly musical setting.
scope: Poetic form does not itself prove or disprove the underlying event. The passage alone cannot date the song’s composition or independently confirm the army’s destruction.

title: Sweetened water without a specified mechanism
summary: The account names a piece of wood and changed water but gives no chemical explanation.
text: Exodus 15:23–25 describes bitter water at Marah becoming drinkable after Moses throws in wood shown to him. Verse 26 connects obedience with a promise concerning diseases brought upon Egypt.
reasoning: The narrative supplies a sequence and theological interpretation, but does not identify the wood, water chemistry, dose or a reproducible treatment.
scope: The passage is insufficient to validate a modern purification method or identify a botanical species. Its promise concerning Egyptian diseases should not be expanded into a universal medical guarantee.

title: Overnight manna and an explicit Sabbath exception
summary: Ordinary leftovers spoil; the portion kept for the Sabbath is explicitly said to remain usable.
text: Exodus 16:19–20 forbids ordinary overnight storage and reports worms and odor when people disobey. Verses 22–26 give different instructions for the sixth day and state that the stored Sabbath portion does not spoil.
reasoning: The account describes an explicit exception with its own instructions. The differing outcomes are not conflicting accounts of one identical storage situation.
scope: This explains the narrative’s rules. It does not establish a natural preservative mechanism, identify manna scientifically or verify the claimed exceptional behavior.

title: A battle is linked to enduring hostility
summary: The account links a battle at Rephidim to a written memorial and continuing war against Amalek.
text: Exodus 17:8–13 describes fighting, Moses’s raised hands and assistance from Aaron and Hur. Verses 14–16 turn the episode into a written memorial, a promise to erase Amalek’s remembrance and war extending across generations. Deuteronomy 25 adds an attack on weary stragglers and commands future erasure of Amalek’s remembrance. Remembering the grievance and erasing the enemy’s remembrance concern different objects, rather than an instruction to forget the command.
reasoning: The transition from a particular battle to continuing hostility is explicit. Joshua fights while others support Moses; the passage assigns different roles rather than attributing victory to only one person.
scope: The narrative does not independently establish troop numbers or the battle’s date. A theological explanation of victory does not constitute an experimentally demonstrated military mechanism or settle the ethical implications of perpetual hostility.

title: Judging disputes becomes a shared responsibility
summary: Jethro challenges Moses’s workload and proposes smaller cases be delegated to other judges.
text: Exodus 18:13–18 describes a queue lasting all day and Jethro’s warning that the arrangement will exhaust both Moses and the people. Verses 19–26 describe teaching, selection of qualified leaders and escalation of difficult cases. Numbers 11 also addresses Moses’s burden through seventy elders, but narrates a divine gift of spirit and prophecy rather than simply repeating the judicial arrangement. Moses declines to prohibit two listed men prophesying in the camp. Deuteronomy 1 recalls shared judging and Moses’s burden without naming Jethro; tribal selection and impartial treatment of resident outsiders are emphasized. Omission of an adviser does not itself deny that adviser’s role in Exodus. Deuteronomy 17 sends difficult cases to priests and a judge at the chosen place, with a death sanction for defiance. This is an escalation procedure, not proof of its enforcement.
reasoning: This is an institutional change inside the narrative, prompted by advice from Moses’s Midianite father-in-law. Verse 23 qualifies the advice with divine command, and verses 24–26 describe its adoption.
scope: The passage provides textual evidence for the institution portrayed. It does not independently verify an administrative system in a dated historical population or establish that the numerical tiers were implemented uniformly.

title: A kingdom of priests still has restricted access
summary: The people are called a kingdom of priests, while the same chapter limits access to the mountain.
text: Exodus 19:5–6 gives a collective covenant designation. Verses 12–13 set a lethal boundary, and 19:21–24 distinguishes Moses, Aaron, priests and the people when regulating approach.
reasoning: A designation for the whole people does not automatically grant every individual the same ritual role or physical access. The chapter itself distinguishes these categories.
scope: This is a possible contextual distinction, not a full reconstruction of how Israelite priesthood developed. The existence of priests in the narrative before later appointment texts requires separate chronological and compositional research.

title: A killing prohibition alongside death penalties
summary: The command against killing appears alongside laws prescribing execution for particular offenses.
text: Exodus 20:13 gives the brief prohibition. Exodus 21:12–17 distinguishes intentional and unpremeditated killing while prescribing death for specified offenses. Exodus 22:18–20 adds other capital prohibitions.
reasoning: The law collection itself does not treat all taking of life as one undifferentiated category. Reading the short command as an absolute ban on every court-ordered death creates tension with its surrounding legal provisions.
scope: This identifies a scope question within the collection. It does not settle the command’s complete lexical history, prove that the penalties were uniformly enforced, or justify these penalties by present-day ethical standards.

title: Burglary rules distinguish circumstances and outcomes
summary: The rules differentiate a thief killed during a break-in, daylight liability and different restitution amounts.
text: Exodus 22:1 requires larger restitution for stolen animals killed or sold; 22:4 requires double when recovered alive. Verses 2–3 distinguish a fatal break-in encounter from one after sunrise, and describe restitution and sale when the thief cannot pay.
reasoning: Different penalties apply to expressly different conditions. Treating fivefold, fourfold and double restitution as rival versions of one identical case ignores those conditions.
scope: These are ancient legal provisions as presented in the text, not present-day legal advice. The text alone does not independently establish enforcement frequency or the precise rationale for every distinction.

title: Protecting the poor without favoritism in court
summary: The laws prohibit both favoring a poor litigant and denying the poor fair judgment.
text: Exodus 23:1–3 rejects false testimony, following a crowd into injustice and favoring a poor person in a case. Verses 6–8 forbid distorting a poor person’s judgment, false charges and gifts that corrupt judgment.
reasoning: The two instructions distinguish social status from the merits of a case: neither favoritism nor deprivation of justice is permitted. Their proximity supplies context for the apparent opposite emphasis.
scope: The provisions express an ideal of judgment. Their presence does not independently prove that actual courts followed it or erase inequalities elsewhere in the law collection.

title: The covenant is narrated through reading and blood
summary: Written words, public assent, an altar and blood mark the covenant ceremony.
text: Exodus 24:3–8 describes the people agreeing, Moses writing and reading the covenant words, sacrifices, and blood applied to the altar and people. The account presents assent and ritual together.
reasoning: The narrator links the obligations to a public ceremony rather than depicting the covenant only as a private experience. The passage attributes writing to Moses, but that narrative attribution is different from externally verifying authorship of the surviving book.
scope: The text alone cannot authenticate the ceremony as a dated historical event, reconstruct every ritual detail or establish the authorship and transmission of the final literary work.

title: The image prohibition and commanded cherubim
summary: The law prohibits images and their worship; sanctuary instructions also require cherubim.
text: Exodus 20:4–5 prohibits making likenesses and bowing to or serving them. Exodus 25 orders two golden cherubim, while chapter 26 places cherubim on fabric. The calf narrative explicitly includes worship and sacrifice; Exodus 34:17 again prohibits molten gods. The construction narrative also describes making the prescribed cherubim.
reasoning: The commands create a real interpretive question for a ban understood to prohibit every depiction. Reading the prohibition as directed at cult images or worship distinguishes these sanctuary decorations, but that is an interpretation of its scope.
scope: This comparison identifies the wording and a contextual reading; it does not establish that every ancient reader applied the same distinction or settle the ethics of religious imagery.

title: Ten curtains and eleven curtains describe different layers
summary: The differing curtain totals refer to linen and an outer goats’ hair covering.
text: The first set has ten linen curtains, each 28 cubits long. The next set has eleven goats’ hair curtains, each 30 cubits long, with surplus folded or hanging over the structure. Exodus 36 repeats the two material layers and their different totals in its construction account.
reasoning: The passage names different materials and describes the second set as a covering. Treating both totals as counts of one identical set removes those contextual distinctions.
scope: This resolves that particular numerical comparison within the instructions. It does not independently verify construction or establish the precise modern length of a cubit.

title: Continual service includes recurring morning and evening duties
summary: The stated schedules help explain language about continual lamps, offerings and incense.
text: Exodus specifies evening-to-morning lamp care and recurring morning and evening offerings and incense. Leviticus repeats the lamp schedule and calls the weekly arrangement of bread continual.
reasoning: Continual observance can include scheduled repetition. The wording alone does not establish uninterrupted 24-hour lamp operation.
scope: This concerns ritual instructions, not proof of historical observance or a technical reconstruction.

title: Priestly clothing represents the tribes
summary: Tribal names appear on shoulder stones and the breastplate as memorials.
text: Chapter 28 connects engraved names on two shoulder stones and twelve breastplate stones with Aaron bearing Israel’s names before God. It also names the Urim and Thummim. Exodus 39 repeats the engraved tribal names and memorial purpose in the construction account.
reasoning: The text supplies a representative purpose for the names, but does not explain the objects or operating procedure of the Urim and Thummim. A precise mechanism would require further evidence.
scope: The symbolism is explicit in the passage. It does not authenticate surviving artifacts, establish exact gemstone identifications or prove a particular divination technique.

title: Ordination uses water, oil, blood and a restricted meal
summary: The ceremony distinguishes priestly consecration from ordinary eating and dress.
text: The instructions combine washing, anointing, blood placed on the right ear, thumb and toe, garments, a sacred meal and seven days of consecration. Outsiders cannot eat the meal; leftovers are burned. Leviticus 8 narrates the corresponding washing, clothing, anointing, blood applications, meal and seven-day consecration. The repeated acts connect instruction with narrated performance without independently verifying it.
reasoning: These actions are presented as consecration. The passage does not assign a separate symbolic meaning to each body part or explain the restrictions as food safety measures.
scope: This describes the ritual as written. Specific symbolic explanations, public health benefits and actual historical performance require additional evidence.

title: The census contribution is a fixed amount
summary: Those counted from age twenty owe the same half-shekel contribution.
text: The passage links counting, a ransom contribution, avoidance of plague and tabernacle service. Rich and poor are assigned the same amount. Exodus 38 reports half-shekel contributions from 603,550 counted men and assigns the silver to sanctuary fittings; this is the narrative’s accounting, not an externally verified census.
reasoning: The contribution is explicitly fixed, rather than proportional to wealth. The plague language is a religious claim within the law, not an independently demonstrated causal link.
scope: This does not establish historical collection rates, modern monetary value or an empirically tested way of preventing disease.

title: Ritual washing is not a stated germ theory
summary: Priests wash hands and feet before service; the passage frames the requirement as sacred duty.
