scope: The exact meaning and handling of the cloth remain interpretive questions. WHO discusses genital examination, not a study of this ancient legal procedure.

sources.label: WHO · Eliminating virginity testing, interagency statement (2018)

title: An exclusion rule and Isaiah’s promise to eunuchs differ in emphasis
summary: Deuteronomy excludes men with specified genital injuries from the congregation; Isaiah promises covenant-keeping eunuchs an enduring place and name.
text: Isaiah 56:3–5 rejects the eunuch’s fear of being a fruitless tree and promises honor within God’s house and walls.
reasoning: Read as an unchanged blanket denial of religious belonging, the exclusion conflicts with the positive promise. A distinction between formal assembly eligibility and promised divine honor, or a change in envisioned circumstances, may explain the difference.
scope: The scope of congregation and the relation between these texts require interpretation. They do not alone establish a complete historical membership policy.

title: Thirty-nine lashes fall within the forty-stripe limit
summary: Deuteronomy sets a maximum of forty stripes; Paul reports five punishments of thirty-nine.
text: Second Corinthians 11:24 identifies thirty-nine lashes on each of five occasions, separately from the rod beatings in verse 25.
reasoning: A maximum permits a lower count. These figures therefore do not contradict each other.
scope: The passages do not explain why thirty-nine was chosen or independently verify Paul’s experiences.

title: An ox-feeding rule becomes an argument for human support
summary: Paul quotes the prohibition on muzzling a threshing ox to argue for workers’ material support.
text: First Corinthians 9:9–14 applies the rule to plowing, threshing and gospel ministry; verses 12 and 15 say Paul has not used that entitlement.
reasoning: An argument for a right and voluntarily declining it are compatible. The passage demonstrates later interpretation of an animal rule.
scope: It does not establish that human ministry was the only original purpose of the Deuteronomy law.

sources.label: 1 Corinthians 9 · quoted rule and support argument

title: Galatians uses the covenant curse in its law-and-faith argument
summary: Galatians quotes the curse on failure to uphold the law within an argument about justification.
text: Deuteronomy closes a communal curse ceremony with assent. Galatians 3:10–14 joins its quotation to statements about faith, Christ and blessing for Gentiles.
reasoning: The shared wording establishes scriptural reuse; the later theological conclusion is an interpretive argument, rather than a second description of the original ceremony.
scope: This comparison neither settles the argument’s theology nor independently dates the ceremony or the texts.

title: A prohibition on returning to Egypt differs from a threatened return
summary: The king must not send people back to Egypt for horses; the covenant curse threatens return to Egypt.
text: Chapter 17 regulates royal action. Chapter 28 presents forced return and attempted enslavement as a threatened consequence of disobedience.
reasoning: A prohibition does not guarantee that the forbidden or feared outcome cannot occur. The shared no-return wording creates tension if read as an unconditional prediction, but the statements have different functions.
scope: This does not identify a specific voyage, establish fulfillment or date the curse.

title: The covenant address includes households, resident outsiders and absent people
summary: The covenant address names leaders, women, children and resident outsiders, then extends beyond those standing there.
text: The passage includes woodcutters and water carriers and expressly says the covenant is not only with the present gathering.
reasoning: This is broader than an address limited to military-age men. Inclusion in this covenant statement does not establish identical legal rights for every category.
scope: The absent group is not precisely identified here. The text is not independent evidence for a dated historical gathering.

title: Romans interprets the nearby commandment as a word of faith
summary: Deuteronomy describes an accessible commandment; Romans reuses its language in a Christ-centered argument.
text: Romans 10:6–9 interprets ascent in relation to Christ, substitutes descent into the deep for Deuteronomy’s sea crossing, and identifies the near word with proclaimed faith.
reasoning: The wording links the texts, while the explanatory referent changes. This is interpretive reuse rather than an identical paraphrase of Deuteronomy’s immediate obedience instruction.
scope: The comparison does not settle Paul’s theology or claim that the original passage explicitly named Jesus.

sources.label: Romans 10 · interpretation of the near word

title: The assurance of presence is followed by an apostasy warning
summary: The chapter promises not to forsake its hearers, then warns of forsaking a people who abandon the covenant.
text: Verses 6–8 encourage the present people and Joshua. Verses 16–18 describe a later turn to other gods and a corresponding withdrawal. Joshua 1:5,9 repeats the presence assurance in Joshua’s commission, while verses 7–8 link success to obeying the law.
reasoning: An unconditional promise for every future circumstance would conflict with the warning. Reading the assurance within covenant loyalty and distinguishing the addressed occasions can reconcile them.
scope: The condition is supplied by the surrounding warning, not stated in the assurance itself. This does not verify historical divine presence.

title: A written law is entrusted for custody and periodic public reading
summary: The narrative attributes law writing to Moses and directs custody beside the ark and a seven-year public reading.
text: The commanded audience includes men, women, children and resident outsiders. The text connects preservation with hearing and learning. Joshua 1:7–8 presupposes a written law for Joshua’s obedience. Deuteronomy 34:5–6,10 narrates Moses’s death and uses retrospective time language.
reasoning: A narrative attribution to Moses is evidence of the authorship claim made within the book, rather than external verification of the surviving book’s complete composition. The closing narrator’s perspective must be distinguished from the earlier law-writing attribution; this distinction alone does not identify an author, editor or date.
scope: This does not identify the deposited manuscript, establish its survival or show how regularly the reading occurred.

title: The song’s rain, rock and blood language uses explicit figurative signals
summary: The song compares instruction to rain, calls God a rock, describes grape juice as blood and depicts drunken arrows.
text: Verse 2 explicitly likens speech to rain and dew; verse 44 identifies the preceding speech as a song.
reasoning: These signals support figurative interpretation of the selected phrases rather than treating them as claims that words are liquid, God is a mineral or arrows metabolize alcohol.
scope: This does not make every statement in the song metaphorical or establish the physical truth of its separate event claims.

title: Levi’s blessing differs from Jacob’s rebuke
summary: Genesis rebukes Simeon and Levi together; Deuteronomy gives Levi a positive priestly blessing and no separate blessing named for Simeon.
text: Genesis 49:5–7 condemns their violence and predicts dispersal. Deuteronomy 33:8–11 instead emphasizes Levi’s covenant loyalty, teaching and sacrifice.
reasoning: The tribal portraits differ, but praise for a later role does not logically deny earlier wrongdoing. The two speeches also have different speakers and narrative occasions.
scope: The omission is a feature of this blessing’s list, not proof that Simeon ceased to exist or a secure date for the poem. Historical explanations need further evidence.

title: Moses’s inability to lead and his undiminished vigor
summary: Moses says he can no longer go out and come in; the ending says his sight and vigor remained intact.
text: Deuteronomy 31:2 pairs his age and inability with the prohibition on crossing Jordan. Deuteronomy 34:7 describes his condition at death.
reasoning: If the first statement means physical debility, the later description creates a tension. A reading about completing leadership duties or permission to lead across Jordan can distinguish the claims.
scope: The leadership reading is contextual, not an explicit definition supplied in verse 31:2. These passages alone do not independently establish his age or medical condition.

title: Twelve stones at Gilgal and twelve in the river
summary: Joshua 4 places carried stones at Gilgal and also describes stones set in the Jordan.
text: Verses 3,8 and 20 connect the carried stones with the campsite and Gilgal. Verse 9 separately attributes a placement at the priests’ standing place to Joshua.
reasoning: The locations conflict only if both descriptions refer to the same single set. Reading verse 9 as an additional set accommodates the wording, though the narrative does not explicitly call it a second set.
scope: This is a possible reading of the received text, not proof that either monument survives or that an editorial history has been established.

title: An eighth-day command and a generation left uncircumcised
summary: Joshua reports that wilderness-born males were not circumcised, despite the earlier eighth-day command. This is a gap between instruction and reported practice.
text: Genesis 17 requires male circumcision, specifies the eighth day and treats remaining uncircumcised as covenant breach. Leviticus 12:3 repeats the timing. Joshua 5:5,7 says those born during the wilderness journey were not circumcised and describes Joshua circumcising them at Gilgal. The second time in 5:2 refers in context to another generation-wide action, not necessarily a second operation on already circumcised individuals.
reasoning: A command does not entail that everyone obeyed it. Joshua distinguishes the circumcised group that left Egypt from their uncircumcised children and supplies a later remedy; it does not issue an opposite command or explain why the earlier timing was not followed.
scope: The omission is expressly reported, but its motive and duration for each individual are not supplied. Do not infer that the eighth-day rule was formally repealed, that every person was circumcised twice, or that these verses independently establish the chronology or historical occurrence.

title: Achan’s household and individual punishment
summary: Achan’s children are included in the judgment scene, while Deuteronomy forbids executing children for a parent’s sin. The narrative does not state their individual guilt.
text: Joshua 7 begins with one named man taking prohibited spoil but attributes a trespass to Israel and connects it to the army’s defeat. Achan confesses his own action. Verse 24 lists his sons and daughters among those brought to Achor; verse 25 first describes stoning him and then uses plural objects for burning and stoning. Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids putting children to death for fathers and assigns death to each person’s own sin. Joshua 22:20 recalls that Achan did not perish alone and that wrath affected the congregation. Joshua 7:5 has already reported roughly thirty-six soldiers killed in the defeat. The later recollection confirms wider fatal consequences; it does not name each additional person or separately describe the death or guilt of each child. Verse 15 announces destruction of the offender and all he has, without separately naming the children. Brenton’s Greek-based English translation of verse 25 retains the singular stoning action but lacks the additional plural burning/stoning clause used by the packaged translations. It still includes sons and daughters in the group brought to the valley in verse 24. Original-language wording of 7:25: the KJV has “burned them with fire, after they had stoned them with stones”; the Hebrew (WLC) has וַיִּרְגְּמ֨וּ אֹתֹ֤ו כָל־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֶ֔בֶן וַיִּשְׂרְפ֤וּ אֹתָם֙ בָּאֵ֔שׁ וַיִּסְקְל֥וּ אֹתָ֖ם בָּאֲבָנִֽים [all Israel stoned him … burned them … stoned them]. In the Brenton Greek, verse 25 ends with Joshua’s words and the next verse has only the singular: Καὶ ἐλιθοβόλησαν αὐτὸν λίθοις πᾶς Ἰσραὴλ [and all Israel stoned him with stones]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/7/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS07.htm.
reasoning: Reading the plural action as extending to the listed family creates tension with the individual-punishment rule. The passage does not explicitly accuse the children of sharing Achan’s theft. Assuming their complicity supplies a fact not stated in this scene. Distinguishing exceptional divine judgment from ordinary legal proceedings is a proposed difference of scope, not an explicit explanation of each family member’s responsibility here. The retrospective statement therefore cannot settle the household question by itself: the earlier military deaths are also part of the narrative consequences.
scope: The final actions do not itemize each victim, so do not claim the text separately describes every child’s execution. The household-inclusive reading is a qualified interpretation of the listed group and plural wording. The collective military consequences and the execution rule are related but not identical kinds of responsibility. No independent historical occurrence or geological mechanism is established. The plural-action argument depends on the longer wording in the packaged editions; Brenton illustrates a different textual tradition without settling priority or the fate of every family member. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier.

title: Thirty thousand and about five thousand in the ambush account
summary: Joshua 8 describes thirty thousand sent for an ambush, then about five thousand placed west of Ai. Whether these are separate detachments is not explicit.
text: Joshua 8:3 names thirty thousand selected fighters, followed by instructions to lie behind the city. Verse 9 locates the ambush west of Ai between Ai and Bethel. Verse 12 then reports about five thousand set in ambush between the same places, west of the city; verse 13 distinguishes the northern army from those lying west.
reasoning: If the two descriptions count the same ambush group, the numbers differ substantially. Reading five thousand as an additional or smaller detachment may distinguish the groups, but the passage does not label it a second ambush or state that it is a subset of the thirty thousand. The later account of the ambush rising in verse 19 does not independently settle the two earlier counts.
scope: This flags an ambiguity within the supplied KJV/WEB/ASV narrative, not a proven census discrepancy. No manuscript comparison, ancient troop count, excavation result or composition history is established by these verses alone. Do not present an inferred additional detachment as expressly stated.

title: A forbidden covenant and a binding oath
summary: The local Gibeonites receive an oath of protection despite the ban on covenants with their people. Joshua explains the deception and the decision to honor the oath.
text: Joshua 9 identifies the visitors as Hivites. They claim distant origins; Israel makes peace without seeking divine counsel, then discovers they are neighbors. Leaders preserve their lives because of the sworn oath and assign compulsory service. Deuteronomy 7 forbids covenants with named local peoples; Deuteronomy 20 distinguishes distant cities from those peoples. Joshua 11:19 reiterates Gibeon as the peace-making exception.
reasoning: The account acknowledges the local-versus-distant distinction. It reports a prohibited agreement followed by concern about breaking an oath, rather than issuing two opposite covenant commands. The survival exception also qualifies an unqualified claim that every local inhabitant was killed.
scope: A tension between prescribed policy and narrated conduct, not proof the laws contradict themselves. Deception and the oath explain the narrative decision; they do not independently establish legal validity, historical occurrence, or the justice of compulsory service.

title: A day with delayed sunset
summary: A literal extra day before sunset departs from ordinary Earth rotation. The account gives no physical mechanism; reading the battle language as poetry changes what is being assessed.
text: Joshua addresses the Sun and Moon, and the account describes a delayed sunset of about a day while attributing the victory to divine action. NASA describes Earth rotating approximately once every 23.9 hours while orbiting the Sun.
reasoning: Ordinary apparent daily solar motion is associated with Earth rotation; merely describing the Sun as moving is not the discrepancy. The issue is a literal extension of daylight beyond that cycle, which is not explained by ordinary rotation. The passage cites Jasher and contains elevated battle language, making interpretation relevant.
scope: This conditional comparison does not show Earth stopped rotating, calculate physical consequences, identify a historical date, or disprove supernatural intervention. NASA supplies the ordinary physical model, not a reconstruction of this battle. A figurative reading does not assert the same physical event.

sources.label: Joshua 10: Sun, Moon and delayed sunset

title: Town lists and their stated totals
summary: Counting compound names together, Judah’s southern list has 36 towns against a total of 29; Naphtali’s fortified-city list has 16 against 19. Some other totals depend on alternative names.
text: Verses 21–32 give 38 comma-separated name entries in the packaged KJV, excluding the explicit Hazor alias. WEB joins the four names in verse 25 into two compound names, yielding 36 towns; both editions state 29. Verses 33–36 give 15 separately named entries in KJV but state 14; WEB treats Gederah/Gederothaim as alternative names, yielding 14. In Joshua 19:2–6 the packaged KJV separately lists Beersheba and Sheba, giving 14 names against 13. WEB treats Sheba as an alternative name, giving 13. The publisher’s eBible KJV page also uses an alternative-name wording here, unlike this packaged KJV dataset. At 19:35–38 both packaged KJV and WEB list 16 fortified-city names, while the stated total is 19; adjacent verses describe boundary locations separately.
reasoning: The southern discrepancy remains after the two compound names are recognized. The NET translator note likewise counts 36 against 29 and proposes alternative names or later additions as explanations. These are proposals, not a verified restoration. The second subtotal illustrates why punctuation alone cannot establish how many distinct places a list identifies. The Naphtali subtotal therefore requires an explanation of which places its total includes or how the list was transmitted. Boundary points should not automatically be counted as additional fortified cities. The differing Sheba wording demonstrates why counts must specify the edition being assessed.
scope: This compares the displayed lists with their subtotals; it does not identify the original manuscript reading or establish ancient administrative boundaries. Joshua 19 says Simeon received part of Judah, but does not explicitly revise this total. No textual correction is made to the packaged Bible. No omitted Naphtali towns are supplied and no manuscript omission is established by the arithmetic alone.

sources.label: Joshua 15: WEB compound and alternative names
Joshua 19: WEB lists and boundary descriptions

title: Hornets and victory without sword or bow
summary: Joshua credits displacement to a hornet rather than Israel’s weapons, while the same speech mentions fighting. The tension depends on whether the weapon denial excludes combat or emphasizes divine agency.
text: Joshua 24:12 attributes displacement to a hornet rather than Israel’s sword or bow, referring to two Amorite kings without naming them. The same speech says the eastern Amorites and Jericho’s people fought Israel (24:8,11). Identifying the two kings as Sihon and Og follows the usage in Deuteronomy 3:8, but is an inference; verse 12 follows the western-Jordan events in verse 11. Deuteronomy 2:32-34 and 3:1-8 describes Israel striking Sihon and Og in battle while crediting divine delivery. Exodus 23:28 promises hornets. Brenton’s Greek-based English translation instead reads twelve kings at Joshua 24:12. KJV 24:12 reads “the two kings of the Amorites”, as does the Hebrew (WLC): שְׁנֵ֖י מַלְכֵ֣י הָאֱמֹרִ֑י. The Brenton Greek edition prints δώδεκα βασιλεῖς τῶν Ἀμοῤῥαίων [twelve kings of the Amorites]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/24/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm.
reasoning: If the weapon denial means no Israelite fighting occurred, it conflicts with Deuteronomy’s battle reports. If it contrasts the ultimate cause of victory with self-reliance, human fighting and divine aid can coexist. The wording does not itself establish which reading is intended.
scope: The comparison does not establish whether hornet is literal, figurative, a particular natural event or a separate stage of displacement. No insect species, military chronology or independent historical event is identified. The two kings are not explicitly identified here. Brenton is a translation witness, not a critical apparatus establishing which original reading is earlier. Its twelve-kings wording limits any unqualified identification with Sihon and Og. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier.

title: Who purchased the burial property?
summary: Joshua and Genesis name Jacob as purchaser of the Shechem land; Acts names Abraham as purchaser of a Shechem tomb. The texts do not explicitly explain the different purchaser.
text: Joshua 24:32 places Joseph’s bones in land at Shechem purchased by Jacob from Hamor’s sons; Genesis 33:19 also names Jacob. Acts 7:15-16 describes a tomb at Shechem purchased by Abraham from Hamor’s sons. Genesis 23 instead narrates Abraham purchasing the Machpelah property from Ephron near Hebron, where Genesis 50:12-13 places Jacob’s burial. In Acts 7:16, the location comes from the statement that the remains were carried to Shechem; the packaged KJV’s closing father-of-Sychem wording can refer to the person rather than the town. If the plural burial subject includes Jacob, Acts’ Shechem location also differs from Genesis 50’s Machpelah burial. If it resumes only the fathers, that particular burial-location conflict does not follow. Original-language wording: Joshua 24:32 (KJV) has “of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for an hundred pieces of silver”; the Hebrew (WLC) has מֵאֵ֛ת בְּנֵֽי־חֲמֹ֥ור אֲבִֽי־שְׁכֶ֖ם בְּמֵאָ֣ה קְשִׂיטָ֑ה [from the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem, for a hundred qesitah]. The Brenton Greek has other sellers and a price in animals: παρὰ τῶν Ἀμοῤῥαίων τῶν κατοικούντων ἐν Σικίμοις ἀμνάδων ἑκατὸν [from the Amorites living in Shechem, for a hundred ewe-lambs]. At Acts 7:16 the KJV ends “of the sons of Emmor the father of Sychem”. The Elzevir Textus Receptus has παρα των υιων εμμορ του συχεμ [from the sons of Emmor of Sychem; no word for “father”]. The SBL and Tischendorf editions have παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἑμμὼρ ἐν Συχέμ [from the sons of Hamor in Shechem]. All three Greek editions name Abraham as the buyer. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/24/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/44/7/, https://bolls.life/get-text/SBLGNT/44/7/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/44/7/.
reasoning: The named purchaser and transaction differ. Treating Abraham and Jacob as interchangeable erases the explicit names. A separate earlier purchase or compressed family history is a possible explanation, but the compared passages do not narrate a second Abraham purchase at Shechem. Acts’ plural burial statement also needs care about which persons it includes.
scope: This establishes a textual comparison, not an archaeological identification of the tombs. Do not claim Joseph was buried at Machpelah or that every patriarch’s burial is separately documented. Original wording, narrative compression and the scope of Acts’ plural subjects require further textual study. The purchaser difference between Acts and Joshua is in the Greek New Testament editions checked, so it is not a product of English translation. title: Sisera’s death in narrative and song
summary: The narrative kills Sisera while he sleeps; the song describes him falling at Jael’s feet. KJV says she struck off his head, while ASV and WEB say she struck through it. A literal sequence needs qualification.
text: Judges 4:21-22 describes Jael driving a tent peg through a sleeping Sisera and into the ground; Barak sees the peg in his temples. title: Moses’ relatives and the in-law label
summary: KJV calls Hobab Moses’ father-in-law; ASV and WEB call him brother-in-law. Exodus names Reuel and Jethro, while Numbers calls Hobab Reuel’s son. The apparent family conflict depends on the kinship reading.
text: Exodus 2:18 names the daughters’ father Reuel, and 2:21 gives Zipporah to Moses. Exodus 3:1 calls Jethro Moses’ father-in-law and priest of Midian. Numbers 10:29 introduces Hobab son of Raguel the Midianite, followed by the in-law label. Judges 4:11 calls Hobab father-in-law in the packaged KJV but brother-in-law in the packaged ASV and WEB. Judges 1:16 associates Moses’ in-law family with the Kenites. Original-language wording: at Judges 1:16 the KJV has “the children of the Kenite, Moses' father in law” and the Hebrew (WLC) likewise gives no personal name: וּבְנֵ֣י קֵינִי֩ חֹתֵ֨ן מֹשֶׁ֜ה. The Brenton Greek supplies one: οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰοθὸρ τοῦ Κιναίου τοῦ γαμβροῦ Μωυσῆ [the sons of Jothor, Jethro, the Kenite, Moses’ in-law]. At Judges 4:11 the Hebrew has חֹבָ֖ב חֹתֵ֣ן מֹשֶׁ֑ה and the Greek Ἰωβὰβ γαμβροῦ Μωυσῆ. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG01.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/4/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG04.htm.
reasoning: If every in-law label denotes the same paternal relationship, the named father and son create tension. Reading Hobab as brother-in-law avoids that particular generation conflict; equating Jethro and Reuel as two names for one person is a possible explanation, not an explicit identification in these passages. Numbers’ punctuation alone does not prove which antecedent receives the label.
scope: This comparison is edition-sensitive. Do not claim all translations make Hobab the father-in-law, or that Kenite and Midianite must be mutually exclusive ethnic identities. No original-language semantic range or family genealogy is established solely from English translations. Alias and clan relationships remain interpretation questions. The Greek of Judges 1:16 names Jethro where the Hebrew and KJV name no one, so in the Greek book both Jethro (1:16) and Hobab (4:11) carry the same in-law word. Brenton’s English renders that Greek word “father-in-law” in both verses; the same Greek word is used for the woman’s father at Judges 19:9, so it does not by itself fix the relationship. title: Seventy brothers, with a survivor?
summary: Judges reports seventy brothers killed while explicitly saying Jotham survived. A precise death count conflicts with that exception; seventy may instead describe the household group.
text: Judges 8:30 gives Gideon seventy sons, then 8:31 adds Abimelech. Judges 9:5 combines the seventy-person killing report with Jotham escaping. Jotham later repeats the number, and the narrator does so at 9:56.
reasoning: If seventy excludes Abimelech but includes Jotham, one survivor leaves at most sixty-nine deaths in that group. If it includes both living men, the maximum is sixty-eight. The repeated seventy is therefore difficult as an exact count of dead brothers. A group total with an explicit exception or a rounded household number is a possible reading.
scope: The text itself identifies the exception. It does not explain its counting convention, so neither sixty-nine nor sixty-eight is established as the actual death toll. This comparison concerns narrative arithmetic, not independent verification of the event.

title: Midian after the campaign in Numbers
summary: Numbers describes killing all Midianite males in its campaign; Judges later has Midian fighting Israel. The tension depends on whether “all” means the entire people or the campaign’s targets.
text: Numbers 31 reports male combat deaths, five kings killed and settlements burned; it then orders the captive boys killed. Its stated grievance concerns Peor. Judges 6–8 portrays Midian participating in a later invasion with Amalekites and eastern peoples.
reasoning: An extinction reading leaves no Midianite males for the later narrative. A campaign-specific reading permits other Midianite groups to remain. The large army figures in Judges 8:10 describe the eastern coalition, not a separately counted wholly Midianite army; the multitude language is not literal infinity.
scope: Neither passage establishes the full geographical extent of Midian or a universal census. No fixed elapsed time, archaeological confirmation or ethnic extinction is established here. This scope comparison is separate from the existing assessment of the treatment of captives.

title: Who sold Joseph to Potiphar?
summary: Genesis names Midianites as Joseph’s sellers to Potiphar, then says Potiphar bought him from Ishmaelites. The different labels could overlap, but the narrative does not explain their relationship.
text: Genesis 37:36 names Midianites at the sale to Potiphar; 39:1 names Ishmaelites as those from whom he bought Joseph. Chapter 37 also mentions both groups in the earlier transfer. Judges 8:24 uses Ishmaelites in a narrative otherwise describing Midian. Genesis traces Midian to Keturah and Ishmael to Hagar.
reasoning: The final seller descriptions differ directly. Distinct ancestral names alone do not establish that later social or trading labels were mutually exclusive. Overlapping labels, allied groups or multiple transfers are possible explanations; none is explicitly explained for the final sale. The subject of the transfer verbs in 37:28 should not be treated as resolving every step.
scope: This is a wording comparison, not proof of incompatible ethnic identities or independent historical evidence. Broader use of Ishmaelite and interwoven-source explanations remain interpretations; the genealogies do not prove exclusive membership of later groups.

title: Chemosh addressed to Ammon’s king
summary: Jephthah calls Chemosh the Ammonite king’s god; Numbers and Kings associate Chemosh with Moab and name a different deity for Ammon. Those associations do not prove exclusive worship.
text: Judges 11 addresses the king of Ammon and calls Chemosh his god. Numbers 21 identifies Moab with Chemosh. Kings distinguishes Chemosh of Moab from Molech or Milcom associated with Ammon.
reasoning: The named association in Jephthah’s speech differs from the other passages. The dispute concerns territory previously attributed to Amorites, and the speech also invokes Moab’s Balak. Referring to a deity associated with the disputed land, overlapping worship, or an inaccurate diplomatic statement are possible explanations; the text does not select one.
scope: This is a comparison of a character’s speech and other textual associations. It does not establish that Ammonites never worshipped Chemosh, identify every deity of either people, or independently verify the historical dispute. No claim about a Greek manuscript or a reconstructed earlier speech is made.

title: Ammon’s land: untouched or allotted?
summary: Deuteronomy says Israel avoided Ammon’s land, while Joshua allots Gad half of it. Jephthah disputes Ammon’s claim. The tension depends on whether the same territory and ownership period are meant.
text: Deuteronomy forbids taking Ammon’s possession and says Israel did not enter it. Joshua 13:25 includes half of Ammon’s land in Gad’s territory. In Judges 11 the king claims land between Arnon and Jabbok; Jephthah says Israel took Amorite territory, not Ammon’s.
reasoning: Read as the same current Ammonite possession, the descriptions conflict. A territorial label reflecting earlier ownership, or land previously transferred to Sihon, could explain them. Numbers 21:26 explicitly describes a prior Moab-to-Sihon transfer, not an equivalent transfer of Ammon’s land; applying that explanation to Ammon is an inference.
scope: Joshua’s allocation does not by itself date an occupation or identify prior ownership at each stage. The opposing diplomatic claims are not an independent boundary survey. These passages do not settle the ancient map, so the proposed ownership distinction remains qualified.

title: The riddle threat: fourth or seventh day?
summary: The KJV places the threat to Samson’s wife on day seven; Brenton’s English Septuagint translation places it on day four. Their descriptions of the answer’s time also differ.
text: Both editions give a seven-day riddle deadline and an answer on day seven. At 14:15 the KJV dates the threat to the seventh day; Brenton prints the fourth. summary: Four times the KJV says Israel went to “the house of God”. The Hebrew has the place name Bethel each time, and so does the Septuagint. In the KJV the ark seems to be at the sanctuary; in the Hebrew and Greek it is at Bethel.

title: Benjamin’s army: mustered, killed and escaped
summary: Benjamin musters 26,700. The dead are given as 25,100 and then as 25,000, and 600 escape. That leaves about 1,000 men unaccounted for. This Septuagint edition musters 23,700 including Gibeah’s 700, fewer than the dead and escaped together.
text: KJV Judges 20:15: “twenty and six thousand men that drew sword, beside the inhabitants of Gibeah, which were numbered seven hundred chosen men” (26,700). 20:35: “twenty and five thousand and an hundred men”. 20:44–45: “eighteen thousand men”, “five thousand men”, “two thousand men”; 20:46: “twenty and five thousand men that drew the sword”. 20:47: “six hundred men turned and fled”. 25,100 + 600 = 25,700; 25,000 + 600 = 25,600; the muster is 26,700. The Hebrew (WLC) has the KJV’s figures: 20:15 עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְשִׁשָּׁ֥ה אֶ֛לֶף [twenty-six thousand]; 20:35 עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וַחֲמִשָּׁ֥ה אֶ֛לֶף וּמֵאָ֖ה אִ֑ישׁ; 20:47 שֵׁ֥שׁ מֵאֹ֖ות אִ֑ישׁ. The Brenton Greek at 20:15 has εἰκοσιτρεῖς χιλιάδες [twenty-three thousand] with the same seven hundred (ἑπτακόσιοι ἄνδρες), 25,100 at 20:35 (εἴκοσι καὶ πέντε χιλιάδας καὶ ἑκατὸν ἄνδρας) and six hundred at 20:47 (ἑξακόσιοι ἄνδρες): a muster of 23,700 against 25,700 dead and escaped. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/20/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG20.htm.
reasoning: These are figures for one army in one chapter. In the KJV and Hebrew about a thousand men are neither killed nor among the survivors, and the day’s dead are stated two ways, 25,100 and 25,000. In the Greek edition the dead and the escaped outnumber the men mustered by two thousand.
scope: Benjamin’s own losses on the first two days are not stated (20:21 and 20:25 give only Israel’s), so a thousand earlier deaths would close the KJV gap; that is a supplied figure, not a stated one. 25,000 may be 25,100 rounded. 20:48 adds further killing in the towns without a number. text: KJV 2 Samuel 5:21: “And there they left their images, and David and his men burned them.” Hebrew (WLC): וַיִּשָּׂאֵ֥ם דָּוִ֖ד וַאֲנָשָֽׁיו [and David and his men lifted them, that is, carried them off]. Aleppo-based edition (HAC): וישאם דוד ואנשיו. The same verb earlier in the book: 2:32 וַיִּשְׂאוּ֙ אֶת־עֲשָׂהאֵ֔ל, KJV “And they took up Asahel”; 4:4 וַתִּשָּׂאֵ֤הוּ אֹֽמַנְתֹּו֙, KJV “his nurse took him up”. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 5:21: καὶ ἐλάβοσαν αὐτοὺς Δαυὶδ καὶ οἱ ἄνδρες [and David and the men took them]. KJV 1 Chronicles 14:12: “David gave a commandment, and they were burned with fire”. Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 14:12: וַיִּשָּׂרְפ֖וּ בָּאֵֽשׁ [and they were burned with fire]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/5/, https://bolls.life/get-text/HAC/10/5/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/4/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA05.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/14/.
reasoning: The Hebrew verb in 2 Samuel 5:21 is the verb for lifting and carrying, which the KJV translates “took up” at 2:32 and 4:4. Burning is a different act, and the Hebrew of Chronicles states it with a different verb and the words “with fire”. The KJV of Samuel therefore says what the Hebrew of Chronicles says, not what the Hebrew of Samuel says. With the Hebrew wording, Samuel has David’s men carry the images off and Chronicles has them burned at David’s order.
scope: Carrying the images off and then burning them could both have happened; neither book says both, and this record does not call the two Hebrew statements incompatible. The finding is the difference between the KJV and the Hebrew and Greek of 2 Samuel 5:21. The Greek agrees with the Hebrew against the KJV, so both H and G apply. title: Hadadezer’s horsemen: 1,700, 700 or 7,000?
summary: The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 8:4 says David took “a thousand and seven hundred horsemen”. The KJV makes that a thousand chariots and seven hundred horsemen. Chronicles and the Greek of Samuel have a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 8:4: “And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen”. Hebrew (WLC): אֶ֤לֶף וּשְׁבַע־מֵאֹות֙ פָּרָשִׁ֔ים וְעֶשְׂרִ֥ים אֶ֖לֶף אִ֣ישׁ רַגְלִ֑י [a thousand and seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand footmen]. Aleppo-based edition (HAC): אלף ושבע מאות פרשים ועשרים אלף איש רגלי. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 8:4: χίλια ἅρματα, καὶ ἑπτὰ χιλιάδας ἱππέων, καὶ εἴκοσι χιλιάδας ἀνδρῶν πεζῶν [a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen]. KJV 1 Chronicles 18:4: “And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen”. Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 18:4: אֶ֣לֶף רֶ֗כֶב וְשִׁבְעַ֤ת אֲלָפִים֙ פָּֽרָשִׁ֔ים [a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/8/, https://bolls.life/get-text/HAC/10/8/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA08.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/18/.
reasoning: In the Hebrew of Samuel there is no word for chariots between “a thousand” and “seven hundred”; the two numbers join into one figure for horsemen. The KJV divides them into two groups, which changes the count of horsemen from 1,700 to 700 and adds a count of chariots. Chronicles, in Hebrew and in the KJV, has a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen, and so does Brenton’s Greek of Samuel. The footmen are twenty thousand in all of them.
scope: H: the KJV count of horsemen differs from the Hebrew count. G: the Greek count of horsemen (seven thousand) differs from the KJV count (seven hundred); here the Greek does not agree with the Hebrew either. The end of the Hebrew verse does mention chariots, so the record does not say none were taken; it says the Hebrew gives no number for them. No claim is made about which figure is original. title: Eighteen thousand in the valley of salt: Syrians, or Edomites?
summary: In 2 Samuel David strikes eighteen thousand Syrians in the valley of salt. In 1 Chronicles Abishai strikes eighteen thousand Edomites there. The Greek of 2 Samuel has Idumea, not Syria.

Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/8/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA08.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/18/.
reasoning: The place and the number are the same in both books. The people struck are Syrians (Hebrew Aram) in Samuel and Edomites (Hebrew Edom) in Chronicles. Brenton’s Greek of Samuel names Idumea, so it differs from the KJV of Samuel on who was struck.

title: How Ishbosheth’s killers got in: fetching wheat, or a sleeping doorkeeper?
summary: In the KJV the two brothers enter “as though they would have fetched wheat” and strike Ishbosheth. In the Greek of that verse a doorkeeper who was cleaning wheat falls asleep and the brothers slip past; no blow is struck until the next verse.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 4:6: “And they came thither into the midst of the house, as though they would have fetched wheat; and they smote him under the fifth rib: and Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.” KJV 4:7: “and they smote him, and slew him, and beheaded him”. Hebrew (WLC) 4:6: לֹקְחֵ֣י חִטִּ֔ים וַיַּכֻּ֖הוּ אֶל־הַחֹ֑מֶשׁ [fetchers of wheat, and they struck him in the belly]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 4:6: Καὶ ἰδοὺ ἡ θυρωρὸς τοῦ οἴκου ἐκάθαιρε πυροὺς, καὶ ἐνύσταξε καὶ ἐκάθευδε· καὶ Ῥηχὰβ καὶ Βαανὰ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ διέλαθον [And behold, the doorkeeper of the house was cleaning wheat, and she nodded and slept; and Rechab and Baana the brothers slipped by]. Brenton Greek 4:7: καὶ τύπτουσιν αὐτὸν, καὶ θανατοῦσιν αὐτὸν [and they strike him and put him to death]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/4/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA04.htm.
reasoning: The KJV of verse 6 has the brothers come in under a pretence, strike, and escape, and verse 7 then tells the killing again. The Greek of verse 6 has no pretence and no blow. It has a doorkeeper, a person the KJV does not mention anywhere in the chapter, and the wheat belongs to her work, not to the brothers’ excuse. The killing itself comes once, in verse 7.
scope: The two accounts of the entry are different, but they are not shown to be incompatible: a doorkeeper could sleep and the brothers could still carry a pretext. The killing in verse 7 is the same in both. No H tag: the KJV follows the Hebrew of verse 6. No claim is made about which form of the verse is older.
